questions.q: Which equation defines v as an eigenvector of matrix A with eigenvalue lambda?
options: Av = lambda * v
A + v = lambda
v = lambda * A
Av = v + lambda
questions.explain: An eigenvector v and its eigenvalue lambda satisfy Av = lambda*v: multiplying v by A gives back the same vector, just scaled by lambda.

questions.q: In the lesson's worked example with A = [[3,1],[0,2]], why is v = (1,1) NOT an eigenvector of A?
options: Av = (4,2), and there is no single scalar that multiplies both entries of (1,1) to give (4,2) -- the two entries would need different scale factors (4 and 2)
Because (1,1) is the zero vector
Because A is not a square matrix
Because eigenvectors can only have positive entries
questions.explain: Av = (4,2) for v=(1,1), but matching (4,2) to a single scalar times (1,1) would require 4/1 and 2/1 to be the same ratio -- they aren't, so no lambda works and (1,1) is not an eigenvector.

questions.q: Geometrically, what does it mean that a vector v is an eigenvector of matrix A?
options: A acting on v only changes its length (or flips its direction exactly 180 degrees) -- it never rotates v into a genuinely new direction
A acting on v always rotates it by exactly 90 degrees
A acting on v always produces the zero vector
A acting on v always doubles its length regardless of the matrix
questions.explain: The defining feature of an eigenvector is that the matrix's action collapses to pure scaling along that direction -- no rotation, whether the eigenvalue is positive, negative, or even zero.

questions.q: Why is the zero vector excluded from being considered an eigenvector, even though A*0 = lambda*0 is technically true for any lambda?
options: Because it would trivially satisfy the equation for every possible lambda, carrying no information about any specific direction the matrix treats specially
Because zero vectors are mathematically undefined
Because matrices cannot be multiplied by the zero vector
Because the zero vector always has a negative eigenvalue
questions.explain: A*0 = lambda*0 holds for literally any lambda, so allowing the zero vector would make the definition meaningless -- eigenvectors are defined to be nonzero so lambda is tied to an actual direction.

questions.q: What did the lesson say eigenvalues correspond to in quantum computing, as a preview of later lessons?
options: The special numbers a measurement of a quantum observable can return -- the same eigenvalue idea from linear algebra, applied to the matrices used in quantum mechanics
The number of qubits in a quantum circuit
The total runtime of a quantum algorithm
The physical temperature of the quantum hardware
questions.explain: The lesson previews that quantum measurement operators have their own special eigenvector directions, and their eigenvalues are literally the only values a measurement of that operator can return -- developed fully in Lesson 19.
